title: Measuring Speed: Benchmarks, -O2, and Assembly
summary: Time code honestly with steady_clock, read the assembly g++ makes, and see what -O2, -O3, and branch prediction do to real loops.
intro: Trading firms argue about speed with numbers, and most quick numbers are wrong: a loop the optimizer deleted, a first run that paid for the operating system's work, a build without optimization. This lesson times code honestly with `std::chrono::steady_clock`, reads the assembly g++ makes to see what really runs, and uses it to explain optimization levels, vectorization, and branch prediction. Every checked output is a checksum or a count, since times change on every run.

steps.title: Timing code with steady_clock

example.title: Converting a price column
example.prompt: Time 5 runs of a currency conversion over 10 million prices, keep the best, and print a checksum.
example.explanation:
`new double[n]` hands back memory that nothing has touched yet, so the first run's writes make the operating system map each 4 KB page as the loop reaches it. Here run 1 took about 15 ms and runs 2 to 5 between 4.4 and 6.1 ms, the best near 4.5 ms, rough times from the emulated sandbox: the first run measured page faults, not the loop. Keeping the best of 5 ignores both that and the noise.

The checksum proves that every conversion happened, and because it's printed, the conversions' results are used, which matters at `-O2`, as the next part shows. Uncomment the two prints to see your own times. They change on every run, which is why this page never checks them.

practice.title: Timing mid prices
practice.prompt:
Time a mid-price pass properly.

1. Time `runs` calls of `mids` with `std::chrono::steady_clock`, pushing each run's milliseconds into `times`.
2. Find the best time with `std::min_element`, and add a commented-out line that would print it.
3. Add every mid price into `checksum`.
4. Between the two lines already printed, print `best <= first: ` and whether the best time is at most the first one.

The input line is `n runs`.

Input:

```text
1000000 5
```

Expected output:

```text
runs timed: 5
best <= first: true
checksum 54249999.75
```

tests.output:
runs timed: 5
best <= first: true
checksum 54249999.75

runs timed: 3
best <= first: true
checksum 10849999.75

runs timed: 8
best <= first: true
checksum 162750000.00

hints: Inside the loop, take `start` and `stop` around `mids(bid.data(), ask.data(), mid, n);` and push `std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>(stop - start).count()`.
`double best = *std::min_element(times.begin(), times.end());` finds the best time.

steps.title: Dead code and constant folding
steps.body:
At `-O2` the compiler may delete or precompute any work whose result the program can't observe. That's what makes optimized code fast, and it's also how a benchmark ends up timing nothing. Two cases catch everyone:

- **A thrown-away result.** If nothing uses what `total(p, n)` returns, and `total` changes nothing else, the call is dead and g++ removes it, loop and all.
- **Inputs it can see.** When the inputs are constants written in the code, g++ does the computation itself while compiling and keeps only the answer. A benchmark on a hard-coded test quote measures a constant.

The assembly shows what really runs. This is part of `main` from the example below, compiled by the sandbox's own g++ at `-O2`:

```text
call   _ZNSt6chrono3_V212steady_clock3nowEv  ; loop 1 starts the clock
call   _ZNSt6chrono3_V212steady_clock3nowEv  ; and stops it, nothing between
call   _ZNSt6chrono3_V212steady_clock3nowEv  ; loop 2 starts the clock
pxor   xmm3, xmm3
mov    eax, 100                              ; 100 runs
movsd  xmm0, QWORD PTR .LC3[rip]             ; 9.0: total(test_quote, 4), worked out already
movapd xmm2, xmm3
.L11:
addsd  xmm2, xmm0                            ; folded += 9.0
sub    eax, 1
jne    .L11
```

To read it: each line is one instruction, destination first, so `sub eax, 1` means `eax -= 1`. `rax`, `rdi`, and their kin (`eax` is the low half of `rax`) are integer registers, and `xmm0` to `xmm15` hold doubles. `QWORD PTR [rdi]` is the 8 bytes at the address in `rdi`. `.L11:` is a label, `jne` jumps back to it until the count reaches zero, `call` calls a function by its mangled name, and `ret` returns. Your terminal shows the same with `g++ -O2 -S -masm=intel file.cpp`.

So benchmark the way the code is really used: on data the compiler can't predict, built at run time or read from input, with every result summed into a checksum you print.

example.title: Three benchmarks, one honest
example.prompt: Time a sum over a million sizes three ways: with its result thrown away, on a constant test quote, and on real data.
example.explanation:
All three loops compile and run, yet only one measures anything. Loop 1 throws its results away, so `-O2` deleted it: the assembly calls `steady_clock::now()` twice with nothing between, and it timed about 0.0002 ms. Loop 2 uses its results, but `test_quote` is a constant the compiler can see, so it worked out `total(test_quote, 4)` itself, 9, and the loop only adds 9.0 a hundred times, hence the 900. Loop 3 runs over a million sizes built at run time and keeps every result, and its 100 runs took roughly 70 to 90 ms in this emulated sandbox, under a millisecond each.

Both totals are printed, so neither loop's results can be dropped. Repeating identical input also measures caches that the previous run left warm, which real traffic may not, so vary the input when that matters.

practice.title: A threshold sweep
practice.prompt:
Fix a benchmark that sweeps the spread threshold.

1. Add each run's count to `checksum`, so no run's work can be thrown away.
2. Give each run a different threshold, `0.25 * (run % 6)`, so the runs sweep from 0 to 1.25 instead of measuring one case again and again.
3. Print `checksum ` and its value after the `runs:` line.

The input line is `n runs`.

Input:

```text
1000000 12
```

Expected output:

```text
runs: 12
checksum 6999992
```
hints: Replace the call's line with `checksum += count_wide(spread.data(), n, 0.25 * (run % 6));`.
`run % 6` cycles through 0 to 5, so the threshold cycles through 0, 0.25, and so on up to 1.25.

steps.title: Optimization levels and vectorization
steps.body:
The level you build at changes your code more than most edits do. This sandbox builds at `-O0` unless a file's first line is `// -O2` (or `-O1`, `-O3`, `-Os`). In your terminal it's the flag itself: `g++ -O2` on Linux, `clang++ -O2` on a Mac, `/O2` with MSVC. Release builds usually use `-O2` or `-O3`.

- **`-O0`** compiles each line as written, for debugging: every variable lives in memory, and every `v[i]` and every step of a range-for is a call into `std::vector`'s code.
- **`-O2`** adds **inlining**, pasting small functions' bodies where the calls were, then keeps values in registers, folds constants, and deletes dead code. The calls into `std::vector` disappear: a range-for, an index loop, and a pointer loop all become the same four instructions.
- **`-O3`** adds **vectorization**: SIMD instructions that work on a whole 16-byte `xmm` register, 2 `int64_t`s or 2 `double`s per instruction. g++ 10.2 vectorizes only at `-O3` (g++ 12 started doing some at `-O2`), while clang on a Mac does it at `-O2`.

The inner loop of `sum_pointer` from the example, from the sandbox's g++:

```text
-O2, one number per trip        -O3, two per trip
.L14:                           .L26:
add rax, QWORD PTR [rdi]        movdqu xmm2, XMMWORD PTR [rax]
add rdi, 8                      add    rax, 16
cmp rdi, rdx                    paddq  xmm0, xmm2
jne .L14                        cmp    rax, rdx
                                jne    .L26
```

And from Apple clang at `-O2` on a Mac (ARM64), eight numbers per trip in four registers:

```text
LBB2_5:
ldp    q4, q5, [x8, #-32]
ldp    q6, q7, [x8], #64
add.2d v0, v4, v0
add.2d v1, v5, v1
add.2d v2, v6, v2
add.2d v3, v7, v3
subs   x10, x10, #8
b.ne   LBB2_5
```

A sum of `double`s stays one at a time even at `-O3`: SIMD would add them in a different order, which changes the rounding, and g++ only allows that with `-ffast-math`. The lesson on bit tricks and SIMD, later in this section, goes further, down to writing SIMD by hand.

> Gotcha: `#pragma GCC optimize("O2")` at the top of a file built at `-O0` looks like the same thing, but g++ then optimizes each function and inlines none, so a range-for still calls the vector's code at every step.

example.title: Three loops, one speed
example.prompt: Sum 10 million sizes with a range-for, an index loop, and a pointer loop, timing each with a best-of-5 helper.
example.explanation:
All three sums agree, and at `-O2` they cost the same: about 4.2 ms each here, timed with `best_ms` (rough, since the sandbox runs emulated). Delete the first line to build at `-O0`, and the range-for takes about 70 ms, the index loop 38 ms, and the pointer loop 8 ms, since every iterator step and every `v[i]` is a real call. Change it to `// -O3`, and all three drop to about 2.7 ms with `paddq`. With the pragma in place of the line, the range-for still took about 40 ms.

So at `-O2` the clear version costs nothing, and you write the loop that reads best. `best_ms` is a function template that takes the work as a lambda and runs it 5 times. The lambdas capture by reference and store each sum in `a`, `b`, and `c`, so the results are printed and the work can't be dropped.

practice.title: Spread cost three ways
practice.prompt:
Write two more versions of a spread-cost loop and check that all three agree.

1. Write `spread_cost_index(const std::vector<Tick>& ticks)`, the same sum as `spread_cost_range`, reading `ticks[i]`.
2. Write `spread_cost_pointer(const Tick* p, std::size_t n)`, the same sum again, reading `p[i]`.
3. Print both results after the range-for line, the pointer version called with `ticks.data()` and `ticks.size()`.

The input is `n`.

Input:

```text
1000
```

Expected output:

```text
range for: 1997.25
index:     1997.25
pointer:   1997.25
```
hints: Both functions start from `double cost = 0;` and loop `for (std::size_t i = 0; ...; ++i)`, to `ticks.size()` or to `n`.
The body is the same in both: `cost += (x.ask - x.bid) * x.bid_sz;`, with `x` being `ticks[i]` or `p[i]`.
Call the pointer version as `spread_cost_pointer(ticks.data(), ticks.size())`.

steps.title: Branch prediction and branchless code
steps.body:
A CPU runs far ahead of the instruction it's finishing, so at every `if` it guesses which way the branch will go and keeps working down that path. A right guess costs almost nothing. A wrong one throws the work away, roughly 15 to 20 cycles on a modern CPU. The predictor learns patterns: in sorted data a test like `size >= 128` is false for a long stretch, then true for the rest, so it's nearly always right. In shuffled data it's a coin flip, wrong half the time.

**Branchless** code turns the decision into arithmetic, so there's nothing to guess. A comparison is a `bool`, which converts to 0 or 1:

```cpp
int size = 150;
std::size_t kept = 0;
kept += size >= 128;
std::cout << kept << '\n';  // 1
```

A filter that copies block trades into a buffer can write every size and move the output forward only for the ones it keeps. Check the assembly before rewriting anything, because g++ often does this for you. For `if (size[i] >= 128) total += size[i];` g++ 10.2 at `-O2` emits `cmovg`, a conditional move with no jump, so sorted and shuffled sizes both took about 5.2 ms per 10^7 here. Only at `-O0`, where the jump stays, did shuffled data cost about 42 ms against 8 sorted. Those times are rough, since the sandbox runs x86-64 emulated. A conditional store is different: g++ keeps the jump, and that's where branchless code pays.

Branchless isn't free. It always does the work of both paths, so a branch that's nearly always predicted right, like an error check or a rare event, is faster as a plain `if`. Measure both on realistic data. You rarely control its order: a feed's sizes arrive in the market's order, not sorted.

The example needs shuffled sizes that are the same on every run, so it draws them from `std::mt19937` in `<random>`. It's an **engine**: it turns a **seed** into a long, fixed sequence of 32-bit numbers, one per call, the same on every run and with every compiler, since the standard fixes the algorithm:

```cpp
std::mt19937 rng(42);  // the engine, seeded with 42
std::cout << rng() << ' ' << rng() << ' ' << rng() % 256 << '\n';  // 1608637542 3421126067 92
```

**Distributions** like `std::uniform_int_distribution<int>(0, 255)` shape those numbers into a range, but each library computes them its own way, so a Mac's libc++ can disagree with libstdc++. `rng() % 256` stays identical everywhere.

example.title: Block trades, sorted and shuffled
example.prompt: Copy the block trades out of 10 million shuffled sizes and the same sizes sorted, with a branchy and a branchless filter.
example.output:
branchy, shuffled:    4998078
branchy, sorted:      4998078
branchless, shuffled: 4998078
branchless, sorted:   4998078
example.explanation:
All four calls find the same 4,998,078 block trades, so the output proves the two versions agree. The times are the point, from `best_ms`, the best-of-5 helper from the previous part, at `-O2` (rough and emulated): the branchy filter took about 27 to 29 ms on shuffled sizes and 4 to 5 ms on sorted ones, while the branchless filter took about 6.5 ms on both. That's a little slower than the branchy one when every guess is right, and 4 times faster when half of them are wrong. The sandbox's g++ shows why:

```text
branchy                           branchless
cmp eax, 127                      cmp   edx, 127
jle .L73                          mov   DWORD PTR [rcx+rax*4], edx
mov DWORD PTR [rcx+r8*4], eax     setg  dl
add r8, 1                         add   rdi, 4
                                  movzx edx, dl
                                  add   rax, rdx
```

The branchy loop's `jle` skips the store whenever the size is under 128, a jump the predictor must guess. The branchless loop has no jump at all: it stores every size, `setg` turns the comparison into 0 or 1, and that's added to `k`. The seeded `std::mt19937` makes the same 10 million sizes on every run, so the count is checked exactly.

practice.title: Cheap offers without a branch
practice.prompt:
Write the branchless version of a filter that keeps the offers priced below a limit.

1. In `below_branchless`, write every price to `out[k]`, then add the comparison `price[i] < limit` to `k`, with no `if`.
2. Leave `main` as it is: it runs both versions on shuffled and sorted prices and prints the four counts.

The input line is `seed n limit`.

Input:

```text
42 1000000 10000
```

Expected output:

```text
branchy, shuffled:    499912
branchy, sorted:      499912
branchless, shuffled: 499912
branchless, sorted:   499912
```

tests.output:
branchy, shuffled:    499912
branchy, sorted:      499912
branchless, shuffled: 499912
branchless, sorted:   499912

branchy, shuffled:    255
branchy, sorted:      255
branchless, shuffled: 255
branchless, sorted:   255

branchy, shuffled:    190081
branchy, sorted:      190081
branchless, shuffled: 190081
branchless, sorted:   190081

hints: The loop body is two lines, like `blocks_branchless` in the example.
First `out[k] = price[i];`, which the next price overwrites when this one isn't kept.
Then `k += price[i] < limit;` moves past the slot only for a kept price.

recap:
- Time with `std::chrono::steady_clock`, never `system_clock`, and convert with `std::chrono::duration<double, std::milli>`.
- Look past the first run, repeat, and keep the best. Checked output holds a checksum, and times go in prose, rough in this emulated sandbox.
- This sandbox builds at `-O0` unless a file's first line is exactly `// -O2` (or `-O1`, `-O3`, `-Os`). In a terminal: `g++ -O2`, `clang++ -O2`, or MSVC's `/O2`.
- At `-O2` the compiler deletes work whose result is unused and computes constant inputs while compiling. Benchmark on real data and sum every result into a printed checksum.
- Read the assembly with `g++ -O2 -S -masm=intel`: destination first, `xmm` registers hold doubles, `call` is a function call, and the `j` instructions are branches.
- `-O2` inlines, so a range-for, an index loop, and a pointer loop compile alike. `#pragma GCC optimize` in a `-O0` build inlines nothing.
- g++ 10.2 vectorizes at `-O3` (`paddq`), clang on a Mac at `-O2`. Sums of doubles need `-ffast-math`, which changes the rounding.
- A mispredicted branch costs roughly 15 to 20 cycles, so a data-dependent `if` is slow on shuffled data. Branchless code turns it into arithmetic, and g++ already uses `cmov` for simple cases, so read the assembly before rewriting.
